ownership_decision.invariant: A paired difference is presented as better or worse only when its interval excludes zero; the verdict is derived from the same paired standard error as the reported interval and travels with it.

boundary_decision.interaction: batch computes the verdict and exposes it through its own HTTP views; the web reads it from the contract and no other context reads it.

domain_forces: A mean with an interval leaves the reader to decide whether a change helped, and a difference whose interval includes zero reads as better when it may be noise.
The interval already comes from the paired standard error, so a second level needs no new statistics.
Fewer than two pairs give no standard error.
implementation_design.decision: pairedDifference returns a verdict beside the mean and the 95% interval; differenceVerdict checks the 99.9% and then the 95% bound on each side; both HTTP views and the contract carry it, and the page shows it first.
invariants_preserved: The mean and the 95% interval are unchanged.
Pairing only test cases judged in both batches is unchanged.
One pair still gives a difference without an interval.
rejected_alternatives: Leaving the verdict to the web, which would put a statistical rule outside the context that owns the numbers.
A noise floor from repeated baseline batches, which needs two batches of one version on the same cases and has no data yet.
implementation_design.counterfactual_check: Use the 95% bound where differenceVerdict checks the 99.9% one; the 0.32 and -0.32 rows of the verdict table must fail. Give a single pair a verdict other than too_few_pairs; the standard-error test must fail.

record.statement: A paired difference between two batches, or between a batch and its skill-withheld arm, is presented as better or worse only when its interval excludes zero: improved or worse when the 99.9% interval does, likely improved or likely worse when only the 95% interval does, no clear difference when the 95% interval includes zero, and too few pairs below two pairs; nothing short of likely improved is presented as an improvement.
examples: A mean of +0.19 with a standard error of 0.1 has a 95% interval that includes zero, so the comparison says there is no clear difference rather than better.
A mean of +0.2 with a standard error of 0.1 is likely improved; +0.33 is improved.
One paired test case gives a difference but too few pairs for a verdict.

record.statement: A paired difference gets a confidence interval only from two or more pairs; one pair gives the difference alone.
examples: One pair gives a difference with no interval.

record.statement: Two batches are compared only on test cases judged in both; a test case judged in only one counts as unpaired, not as better, worse or tied.
examples: A test case judged in the candidate but not the reference adds to unpaired.
